clue.text: Wealthy woman, not healthy one, broadcasting during disorder

indicators.note: something that happens during a period sits inside it, so these words go within the outer piece

blocks.note: someone not healthy is ill
the Roman numeral for one
a programme being broadcast is on air
a mess is a state of disorder

explanation.surface: A rich woman, sickly companion in tow, is putting her views out to the world amid chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make 'not healthy one' look like a description of the woman, but it is two separate pieces of wordplay, and 'broadcasting' is a state, not an action.
explanation.definitionFit: A millionairess is a female with a fortune of at least a million, a plain synonym for a rich lady.

clue.text: Encroachment of over ten dogs into pub

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece written over another sits above it, so the dogs come first
putting things into a place sets them inside it, so the pub wraps round the rest

blocks.note: curs are mongrel dogs
ten written as figures, 1 and 0, read as the letters I and O
an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: A complaint about a pack of more than ten dogs invading the local.
explanation.walkthrough: Ten is read as its figures, 1 and 0, which look like the letters I and O; in a down clue 'over' means placed above.
explanation.definitionFit: An incursion is a hostile raid or intrusion into territory, the same idea as trespassing onto it.

clue.text: Best end of crow?

blocks.note: surface reading: the finest final part of a bird, or the tastiest cut of one
setter's reading: to crow is to exult, and the proverb says whoever has the final one of these has the best

explanation.surface: A butcher's question about the choicest cut of a crow, as in best end of lamb.
explanation.walkthrough: Best end is a cut of lamb or mutton, which sets up the butchery picture. The proverb 'he who laughs last laughs best' makes the last laugh the best one, and crowing is gloating.
explanation.definitionFit: To crow is to gloat noisily; the proverb about whoever has the last one makes it the best, so the final burst of mirth wins.

clue.text: Titus went off to sea

indicators.note: something that has gone off has spoiled, so these letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Titus left home and became a sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: Titus Oates was the 17th-century fabricator of the Popish Plot. The surface also nods to Captain Oates, who walked off into the Antarctic snow.
explanation.definitionFit: Titus is the first name of the notorious English perjurer whose surname this is, so the first name stands for the man.

clue.text: Do I learn about relations being divine?

indicators.note: one thing about another goes round it, so the question wraps round the relations

blocks.note: read as 'Am I a L?', that is, am I a learner, with L the learner driver's letter
bros is short for brothers, who are relations

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether studying family ties makes them holy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do I learn?' is rephrased as the question 'Am I a learner?', and the learner becomes L as on a learner driver's plate; the relations split that question after its second word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrosia was the food of the gods, so something ambrosial is heavenly or fit for the gods, which is divine in its loose sense.

clue.text: Film director's children, one going off with chocolate cake

definitions.note: the possessive is the setter's link to the wordplay

indicators.note: one going off leaves, so a single child departs from the word for the brood

blocks.note: taken as written
one of the children is a child, the part that leaves
an eclair is a cream-filled pastry iced with chocolate

explanation.surface: A film director's family: one child walks out, leaving the rest with a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: Take CHILD out of CHILDREN to leave REN, then add ECLAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: René Clair was a celebrated French filmmaker of the 1930s, maker of Le Million and À nous la liberté.

clue.text: Introduce a note and nearly set fire to it?

blocks.note: loosely, to sing is to bring a tune out, to introduce music
E is one of the notes of the scale

explanation.surface: Advice to a singer: bring in a note and almost set the place alight.
explanation.walkthrough: A loose Araucaria clue: singing a note E is the way to introduce one, giving SING plus E. The question mark marks the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: To singe is to burn slightly or scorch the surface, which is coming close to setting something alight.

clue.text: Deal with merry-andrew, who can give you ...

definitions.note: the clue runs on into 9 down: one who can give you a parking ticket

indicators.note: a merry person is tipsy and unsteady, so the name that follows is jumbled

blocks.note: to traffic is to deal or trade
taken as written

explanation.surface: A merry-andrew is a clown, so this reads as handling a buffoon who can give you something.
explanation.walkthrough: A merry-andrew is a clown or buffoon, so the hyphenated word hides the anagram signal and the fodder. The definition finishes in the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a traffic warden is the official who patrols streets and issues fines for illegal parking.

clue.text: ... a parcel containing a royal sovereign - take it up

definitions.note: the definition is shared with 8 down: what a traffic warden can give you

indicators.note: a parcel containing goods holds them inside, so the parcel wraps round the rest
in a down entry, taking a word up means reading it from bottom to top

blocks.note: a packet is a small parcel
R is the abbreviation for royal
a king is a sovereign
taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions about a package holding a royal coin, a sovereign: pick it up.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign is also an old British gold coin, which colours the surface. PACKET holds R, KING and IT read upwards (TI): PA-RKINGTI-CKET.
explanation.definitionFit: A traffic warden hands out fixed-penalty notices for illegal parking, so this is what such an official can give you.

clue.text: Tell (the votes again)

definitions.note: a verb phrase with 'count' understood: count the votes again

blocks.note: first meaning: to narrate or relate a story
second meaning: ..., to tally the ballots a second time

explanation.walkthrough: The brackets hold the second sense: 'tell' also means count, as in a bank teller or 'all told', so telling the votes again is a re-count.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount is to relate a story, and with the stress moved, to re-count is to tally ballots a second time after a close election.

clue.text: France's good day down under unfinished by a stroke of luck

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: bon is French for good
Anzac Day, 25 April, is the Australian and New Zealand day of remembrance

explanation.surface: A French well-wisher's greeting on an Australian holiday, cut short by sudden good fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: Down under means Australia and New Zealand; Anzac Day honours their soldiers of Gallipoli.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonanza, originally a rich vein of ore struck by miners, is any sudden windfall or source of great wealth.

clue.text: Scottish flower is out

blocks.note: first meaning: a river in Scotland, a flower being something that flows
second meaning: onwards or outwards, as in 'go out' or 'set out'

explanation.surface: A thistle or heather that has come into bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords a flower is often a river, something that flows; this one runs past Stirling to its famous estuary near Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: The river gives its name to the Firth and the bridges, and as an adverb the word means outward or away, as in 'sally out'.

clue.text: Random test to identify squared pattern

blocks.note: to spot something is to pick it out
a check is a pattern of squares, as on a tablecloth

explanation.surface: A quick examination to recognise a design made of squares.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot check is an inspection made without warning on a sample chosen at random, rather than a full survey.

clue.text: Dostoievsky's tale told the life of Macbeth

definitions.note: the title of his novel, without the article

definitions.text: tale told the life of Macbeth
definitions.note: the teller of the tale that Macbeth says life is

blocks.note: first meaning: the title character of the Russian novelist's 1869 novel about Prince Myshkin

blocks.clueFragment: tale told the life of Macbeth
blocks.note: second meaning: Macbeth calls life 'a tale told by' one of these, full of sound and fury

explanation.surface: A literary puzzle linking a Russian story with the life of a Scottish king.
explanation.walkthrough: Macbeth's speech runs 'it is a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing'; the clue drops 'by an' so the answer fills that gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The fool is the title figure of Dostoevsky's novel and, in Shakespeare, the narrator of the story that is life.

clue.text: It housed the treasure of the Lizard

definitions.note: the word's Greek root means treasury or storehouse

blocks.note: taken as written
saurus is the Greek-derived word for a lizard, as in dinosaur

explanation.surface: The Lizard is a Cornish peninsula, so this reads as the building where Cornwall's treasure was kept.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lizard is the southernmost point of mainland Britain, in Cornwall, which tempts a reading about local treasure.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek thesauros meant a storehouse or treasury, and a word-book is a treasury of words, so this housed treasure.

clue.text: Wreck of the 15-a-side game by a  type of Toryism

blocks.note: rugby union is played fifteen a side, abbreviated RU
One Nation is a strand of Conservatism, with the one written as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A rugby match ruined by a brand of Conservative politics.
explanation.walkthrough: One Nation Toryism, from Disraeli, is the paternalist wing of the British Conservative Party; Roman I stands for its first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruination is the act or state of being ruined, so it works as a noun for a wreck or destruction.

clue.text: Not a revolutionary creed, that is, of Mr and Mrs Turner

indicators.note: a turner turns things round on a lathe, so the letters get turned about

blocks.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gentle political creed belonging to a married couple named Turner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mr and Mrs Turner' looks like a couple; Turner is the anagram signal, and 'and' merely joins the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Reformism seeks gradual change within existing institutions instead of overthrowing them, the opposite of revolution.

clue.text: US politician, admiral and watchmaker faking liner's log

indicators.note: faking means forging or counterfeiting, so the letters are falsified into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Three American notables accused of forging a ship's record book.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname covers Robert G. Ingersoll the orator and politician, Admiral Royal Ingersoll, and the Ingersoll dollar-watch firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the three people named bore this surname: the free-thinking speaker, the Second World War naval commander and the cheap-clock maker.

clue.text: The West, going to flounder miserably, applied to Copenhagen

definitions.note: the adjective the song applies to the city

indicators.note: doing something miserably means doing it badly, so the fish's letters go wrong

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for west
taken as written

explanation.surface: Western powers struggling helplessly over the Danish capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wonderful, Wonderful Copenhagen' is Danny Kaye's song from the 1952 film Hans Christian Andersen.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Loesser's song lyric calls the Danish capital this, so the adjective is the one that song attaches to it.

clue.text: 15 man producing some-thing of an ego-trip

definitions.note: the man behind the famous word-book

indicators.note: some of something is only part of it, so the tail of the phrase is left behind
producing suggests making something new out of material, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: A man famous for his word-book creating something of a vanity project.
explanation.walkthrough: A loose Araucaria parse: part of 'ego-trip' supplies five letters, which are then rearranged; 15 points to the answer at 15 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Mark Roget compiled the famous Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases in 1852, so he is its man.

clue.text: Exposed again holding diamonds and hearts, so coloured on top

indicators.note: something holding items keeps them inside, so the cards go within

blocks.note: something re-aired has been brought out into the open once more
D is the abbreviation for the card suit
H is the abbreviation for the card suit

explanation.surface: A bridge hand laid out again, showing diamonds and hearts, red cards on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So' links back to the red suits: diamonds and hearts are red, and someone coloured that way on top has hair of that colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with ginger or auburn locks is coloured red on the head, which is the top of the body.

clue.text: I leave 14 with a Greek vase

indicators.note: a letter that leaves goes away, so it is struck out of the word

blocks.note: taken as written: the letter removed
the answer to 14 across
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone takes leave of a fool, carrying an ancient pot.
explanation.walkthrough: The first I goes from the answer to 14 across, then A follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A diota is a two-handled ancient jar or amphora; the name is Greek for two-eared, after its handles.

clue.text: Artist that lasts?

definitions.note: a whimsical noun, a thing that endures

blocks.note: first meaning: the German Renaissance painter and engraver Albrecht
second meaning: read as ..., one that endures, from the verb dure

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags an invented word: to dure is an old verb for to last, so a durer is one that lasts.
explanation.definitionFit: Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg is famous for prints such as Melencolia and the Rhinoceros, and is the artist meant here.

clue.text: Architectural style from Greenland or Iceland

indicators.note: something taken from a phrase is drawn out of it, so the letters lie within these words

blocks.note: spanning the end of the first place, the middle word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A building design imported from one of two northern Atlantic islands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Doric order, with plain capitals and fluted columns, is the oldest and simplest of the classical Greek architectural orders.

clue.text: Do it yourself, badly - no good for ending

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the letters come out in the wrong order

blocks.note: DIY is the usual abbreviation for do-it-yourself
NG is the abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: A home handyman's botched job that turns out useless in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Dying is the process of coming to an end, as a dying fire or a dying tradition, so it can mean ending.

clue.text: French and British princess, the former foolish

definitions.note: 'the former' is French, the first of the two languages named, so this is French for foolish

blocks.note: et is French for and
a British setter writing for British readers calls British things ours
Di was the popular name of Diana, Princess of Wales

explanation.surface: A tale of a French and a British princess, the earlier of whom was silly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The former' looks like it refers to one of the princesses; it actually picks out French, so the definition is a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Étourdi is the French adjective for thoughtless or scatterbrained, so it translates the English word foolish.

clue.text: Looks at the Eternal City as Spooner did in the undergrowth?

indicators.note: Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so the starts of two words are exchanged

blocks.note: looks at is eyes and the Eternal City is Rome; 'eyes Rome' with its opening sounds swapped

explanation.surface: A tourist eyeing Rome with Spooner's tongue-twisting, lost in the shrubbery.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of 'eyes Rome' and you say 'rize ohm'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhizome is a creeping stem that grows horizontally below the soil surface, sending out roots and shoots.

clue.text: Royal chalice - his grammar needs correcting - of some age

definitions.note: a cryptic rewording of kingcup, another name for the plant

indicators.note: something that needs correcting is wrong as it stands, so these letters must be put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
something of some age is old

explanation.surface: An aged king's goblet, and a grumble that his grammar is faulty.
explanation.walkthrough: A king is royal and a cup is a chalice, so 'Royal chalice' is kingcup, the plant's country name.
explanation.definitionFit: The marsh marigold, Caltha palustris, a yellow wetland flower, is also called kingcup, which the clue paraphrases.
